name: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
causingAgent: Early blight - Alternaria solani.
favourableClimate: Warm and Humid conditions (24°C - 30°C / 75°F - 86°F).
symptoms:
1) Foliage: Symptoms typically begin as small, dark brown lesions with concentric rings on older leaves. These lesions often have a target-like appearance.
2) Lower Leaves: The lower leaves of the plant are usually the first to show symptoms, and as the disease progresses, they may die and drop off.
3) Stems and Fruit: Early blight can also affect stems and fruit, causing dark, sunken lesions on the fruit.
4) Spread: The disease is favored by warm and humid conditions, but it can develop under a wide range of environmental conditions.
5) Impact: While early blight is less aggressive than late blight, it can still significantly reduce the quality and yield of tomato plants, especially if not managed properly.
management:
1) Fungicides: Fungicidal treatments can be effective in controlling early blight. Copper-based fungicides (Copper Oxychloride 2.5g/L) and Mancozeb or Azoxystrobin are commonly used.
2) Sanitation: Removal and destruction of infected plant material are essential to reduce the spread of the disease.
3) Crop Rotation: Rotating tomato crops with non-solanaceous crops (plants not related to tomatoes) can help break the disease cycle.
4) Mulching: Mulching around the base of plants can help prevent soil-borne spores from splashing onto leaves.

name: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
causingAgent: Late blight - Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora Infestans.
favourableClimate: Cool and Wet conditions, with temperatures between 10-26°C (50-78°F) and high humidity >85%.
symptoms:
1) Foliage: Symptoms typically start as dark, water-soaked lesions on the leaves, which quickly enlarge and can appear within a few days. These lesions are often surrounded by a pale yellow halo.
2) Stems and Petioles: Stems and petioles can also become infected and exhibit dark brown/black lesions.
3) Fruit: Late blight can infect tomato fruits, causing dark, irregularly shaped firm greasy lesions. Infected fruits rot rapidly.
4) Spread: The pathogen spreads rapidly under cool and wet conditions, transmitted through wind-blown sporangia or rain splashes.
5) Impact: Late blight is one of the most destructive tomato diseases, causing total crop defoliation within days if left unchecked.
management:
1) Fungicides: Application of systemic and contact fungicides (Metalaxyl + Mancozeb, Cymoxanil, Dimethomorph, or Copper Oxychloride).
2) Sanitation: Removing and destroying infected plant material immediately.
3) Spacing: Proper plant spacing and staking to maximize air circulation and reduce foliar humidity.
4) Resistant Varieties: Plant certified resistant hybrid tomato lines.

name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV)
causingAgent: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a single-stranded RNA virus of the Tobamovirus genus.
favourableClimate: Warm and Humid conditions. Transmitted mechanically through hands, tools, and grafting.
symptoms:
1) Mottled Leaves: Foliage displays a mosaic-like pattern with light and dark green blistered patches.
2) Stunting: Infected plants exhibit stunted growth and shortened internodes.
3) Leaf Distortion: Leaf curling, shoe-stringing, and fern-like leaf distortion.
4) Reduced Fruit Quality: Fruits show internal browning, uneven ripening, and surface mottling.
5) Transmission: Spreads rapidly via mechanical contact, tools, seedlings, and contaminated hands.
management:
1) Resistant Varieties: Plant ToMV-resistant tomato varieties (e.g., cultivars with Tm-2/Tm-2a resistance genes).
2) Hygiene & Sanitation: Disinfect pruning shears in 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or bleach solution.
3) Rogueing: Promptly remove and safely burn infected plants.
4) Certified Seeds: Use certified virus-free seeds and avoid tobacco use near greenhouse facilities.

name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
causingAgent: Begomovirus (family Geminiviridae), transmitted vectorially by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
favourableClimate: Warm tropical and subtropical climates (25°C - 35°C) with active whitefly populations.
symptoms:
1) Leaf Curling: Terminal and young leaves curl upright in a cupped or erect position.
2) Chlorosis: Marked interveinal yellowing with pale green or yellow leaf margins.
3) Bushy Stunting: Extreme stunting of upper shoots resulting in a compact, bushy appearance.
4) Flower Abortion: Flowers drop off before fruit set, causing catastrophic yield loss up to 100% in early infections.
management:
1) Vector Control: Install yellow sticky cards (20-30/acre) and spray Diafenthiuron 50 WP (1g/L) or Flonicamid 50 WG (0.3g/L) or Neem oil (1500 ppm).
2) Protected Nurseries: Raise seedlings under 40-50 mesh insect barrier netting.
3) TYLCV Resistant Hybrids: Use modern resistant cultivars containing Ty genes.
4) Rogueing: Immediately eradicate early symptomatic plants.

name: Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)
causingAgent: Soil-borne vascular fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici.
favourableClimate: Warm soil temperatures (25°C - 35°C / 77°F - 95°F) and acidic sandy soils.
symptoms:
1) Unilateral Yellowing: Progressive yellowing starting on lower leaves, often restricted to one side of the plant or branch.
2) Daytime Wilting: Plants wilt during hot sunny afternoons and partially recover overnight.
3) Vascular Ring Browning: Slicing the main stem reveals distinct reddish-brown discoloration in the xylem vascular rings.
4) Plant Collapse: Progressive vascular blockage leads to total plant death.
management:
1) Resistant Hybrids: Choose tomato cultivars with multi-race Fusarium resistance (Fol-1, Fol-2, Fol-3).
2) Soil Treatment: Inoculate seedling root zone with Trichoderma viride / T. harzianum (2.5 kg/ha with FYM).
3) Crop Rotation: Rotate 3-4 years with non-solanaceous crops.
4) Liming: Maintain soil pH around 6.5 - 7.0 using agricultural lime.

name: Verticillium Wilt (Verticillium dahliae)
causingAgent: Soil-borne fungus Verticillium dahliae forming long-lived resting microsclerotia in soil.
favourableClimate: Cool to moderate temperatures (20°C - 25°C / 68°F - 77°F) with alkaline to neutral soil.
symptoms:
1) V-Shaped Chlorosis: Characteristic V-shaped yellow necrotic wedges between main leaf veins starting on older leaves.
2) Wilting & Scorching: Margins turn brown, dry up, and curl, followed by premature defoliation.
3) Vascular Discoloration: Light tan to brown streaking in the lower stem vascular bundles.
4) Stunted Development: Uniform reduction in plant vigor and fruit size.
management:
1) Resistant Cultivars: Plant certified 'V' resistant tomato varieties.
2) Soil Solarization: Solarize moist nursery and field soil under transparent plastic film for 4-6 weeks in summer.
3) Bio-fungicides: Soil application of Trichoderma and Bacillus subtilis.
4) Avoid Root Wounding: Minimize root damage during intercultural hoeing and weeding.

name: Bacterial Speck & Spot (Pseudomonas / Xanthomonas)
scientificName: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato / Xanthomonas vesicatoria
causingAgent: Phytopathogenic bacteria Pseudomonas syringae (Speck) and Xanthomonas vesicatoria (Spot).
favourableClimate: Cool to warm wet weather (18°C - 28°C), high humidity, overhead irrigation, and wind-driven rain.
symptoms:
1) Foliar Specks: Tiny, pinpoint dark brown to black spots (1-2 mm) surrounded by prominent yellow chlorotic halos.
2) Water-soaked Spots: Xanthomonas creates greasy, water-soaked angular spots on leaves and stems.
3) Fruit Scabs: Raised, black scabby specks or white-haloed blisters on green fruit surfaces rendering them unmarketable.
4) Defoliation: Severe leaf spotting causes blighting and premature leaf fall.
management:
1) Copper + Antibiotic Spray: Spray Copper Hydroxide / Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) combined with Streptocycline (0.1 g/L).
2) Disease-Free Seed: Hot water seed treatment (50°C for 25 minutes) before sowing.
3) Drip Irrigation: Avoid overhead sprinklers to prevent bacterial splash dispersal.
4) Field Sanitation: Remove weed hosts and plow under old crop debris.

name: Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea)
causingAgent: Necrotrophic fungus Botrytis cinerea attacking damaged, senescent, or succulent tissues.
favourableClimate: Cool, humid conditions (15°C - 22°C / 59°F - 72°F) with relative humidity >90% and poor air movement.
symptoms:
1) Fuzzy Gray Mold: Prolific velvety gray-brown fuzzy fungal mycelium and conidia on leaves, stems, and fruits.
2) Stem Cankers: Light brown, elliptical girdling stem lesions originating from pruning wounds or dying petioles.
3) Ghost Spots on Fruit: Faint, pale circular rings or halo 'ghost spots' on green fruit surfaces.
4) Soft Watery Rot: Blossom-end fruit decay leading to soft, watery breakdown.
management:
1) Canopy Ventilation: Prune lower suckers cleanly to promote brisk airflow and lower humidity.
2) Fungicides: Spray Boscalid, Iprodione, Pyraclostrobin, or Fluopyram + Tebuconazole.
3) Clean Pruning: Prune only on dry sunny days to allow cut surfaces to heal rapidly.
4) Bio-control: Preventive sprays of Trichoderma viride or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.

name: Septoria Leaf Spot (Septoria lycopersici)
causingAgent: Septoria lycopersici, an ascomycete fungus producing pycnidia.
favourableClimate: Warm and wet conditions (20°C - 26°C / 68°F - 78°F) with frequent rain or dew.
symptoms:
1) Shot-Hole Spots: Numerous small circular spots (2-3 mm) with grayish-white centers and dark brown margins.
2) Black Pycnidia: Tiny black specks (fungal fruiting bodies) clearly visible inside the light center of mature spots.
3) Lower Canopy Defoliation: Progresses rapidly upwards from oldest lower leaves, resulting in complete defoliation.
4) Sunscald on Exposed Fruit: Loss of leaf umbrella exposes green tomatoes to direct sunscald.
management:
1) Preventive Fungicide Sprays: Spray Chlorothalonil 75 WP (2 g/L), Mancozeb (2.5 g/L), or Azoxystrobin (1 ml/L).
2) Bottom Leaf Pruning: Remove infected lower foliage up to 12 inches from ground level.
3) Mulching: Apply straw or plastic mulch to stop rain-splash inoculation from soil.
4) Crop Rotation: Avoid planting solanaceous crops for 2-3 seasons in infected parcels.

name: Powdery Mildew (Oidium spp. / Leveillula taurica)
causingAgent: Obligate foliar fungi Oidium neolycopersici (ectophytic) and Leveillula taurica (endophytic).
favourableClimate: Warm, dry days with high relative humidity at night (20°C - 30°C / 68°F - 86°F).
symptoms:
1) White Powdery Patches: Talcum-like white powdery fungal growth on upper and lower leaf surfaces.
2) Chlorotic Blocs: Bright yellow angular patches on upper leaf surface corresponding to fungal colonies below.
3) Foliar Scorching: Leaves turn yellow, brown, curl upwards, and dry prematurely.
4) Stunted Fruit Sizing: Severely restricts photosynthetic capacity, resulting in small unmarketable fruits.
management:
1) Fungicides: Spray Wettable Sulphur (2.5 g/L), Hexaconazole (1 ml/L), or Difenoconazole (0.5 ml/L).
2) Organic Options: Spray Potassium Bicarbonate (3 g/L) or diluted milk solution (1:9 ratio) or Neem oil.
3) Ventilation: Reduce canopy density in greenhouses and high tunnels.
4) Resistant Cultivars: Select powdery mildew tolerant hybrids.

name: Southern Blight (Sclerotium rolfsii)
causingAgent: Soil-borne necrotrophic fungus Sclerotium rolfsii producing mustard seed-like brown sclerotia.
favourableClimate: High temperatures (28°C - 35°C / 82°F - 95°F) with high soil moisture and organic mulch.
symptoms:
1) Sudden Daytime Collapse: Rapid green wilting and complete plant collapse without prior chlorosis.
2) White Fan Mycelium: Dense, fan-like cottony white mycelial web growing over the lower stem base and soil surface.
3) Brown Sclerotial Beads: Abundant round, tan-to-brown mustard seed-sized resting sclerotia on stem lesions.
4) Collar Rot: Wet, brown rotting and disintegration of stem bark at the soil line.
management:
1) Deep Plowing: Deep turn soil (8-12 inches) to bury sclerotia below root zone.
2) Bio-fungicides: Soil drenching with Trichoderma harzianum and Pseudomonas fluorescens.
3) Fungicide Drench: Drench collar zone with Carbendazim (1 g/L) or Captan (2 g/L) or Azoxystrobin.
4) Remove Diseased Plants: Carefully dig up and discard wilted plants with surrounding soil.

name: Root-Knot Nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.)
causingAgent: Microscopic soil-dwelling endoparasitic roundworms (Meloidogyne spp.).
favourableClimate: Warm soil temperatures (24°C - 32°C / 75°F - 90°F) in sandy or light-textured soils.
symptoms:
1) Swollen Root Galls: Severe swelling, bead-like knots, and irregular galls throughout the fibrous root system.
2) General Stunting & Chlorosis: Yellowing, reduced shoot vigor, and unthrifty stunted growth.
3) Afternoon Wilting: Plants wilt severely during peak sunshine even when irrigation is adequate.
4) Heavy Yield Drop: Reduced fruit set, small fruits, and high vulnerability to vascular Fusarium wilt complex.
management:
1) Resistant Cultivars: Choose nematode-resistant tomato hybrids (Mi gene cultivars).
2) Nematicide Application: Apply Fluopyram 34.48% SC or Cartap Hydrochloride or Paecilomyces lilacinus bio-nematicide.
3) Organic Amendments: Incorporate Neem cake (500 kg/ha) or mustard meal into soil during bed prep.
4) Crop Rotation & Trap Crops: Rotate with marigold (Tagetes patula) or sunn hemp to suppress nematode counts.

name: Powdery Mildew
causingAgent: Pathogen: Erysiphe cichoracearum / Podosphaera xanthii. Obligate biotrophic fungi producing talcum-like conidia.
favourableClimate: Warm and dry conditions (20°C - 30°C / 68°F - 86°F) with moderate humidity and dense vine canopy.
symptoms:
1) White Powdery Patches: Initial small talcum-white powdery spots on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and young stems.
2) Leaf Chlorosis & Browning: As spots coalesce, foliage turns yellow, becomes brittle, and turns brown.
3) Premature Senescence: Extensive infection leads to premature leaf drying and drop, exposing developing gourds to sunscald.
4) Reduced Yield: Inhibits photosynthesis, resulting in stunted vine growth and malformed or bitter gourds.
management:
1) Fungicides: Spray Wettable Sulphur (2g/L) or systemic fungicides like Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole or Hexaconazole (1ml/L) at early symptom appearance.
2) Proper Air Circulation: Provide adequate vine trellis support and spacing to avoid stagnant moisture.
3) Sanitation: Prune and burn infected foliage.
4) Organic Remedies: Diluted milk spray (1 part milk to 9 parts water) or Neem oil (1500 ppm).
5) Resistant Varieties: Plant powdery mildew tolerant cucurbit hybrids.

name: Fruit Fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae)
causingAgent: Species: Bactrocera cucurbitae (Melon Fruit Fly). The female fly punctures young fruits to lay eggs; internal feeding maggots cause tissue decay.
favourableClimate: Warm temperatures (25°C - 35°C / 77°F - 95°F) with high relative humidity and damp field conditions.
symptoms:
1) Egg-Laying Punctures: Small puncture marks or brown oviposition spots on tender fruit skin with resinous oozing.
2) Internal Larval Feeding: Maggots tunnel through the internal fruit pulp, causing brown rot and tissue collapse.
3) Fruit Deformity & Rot: Fruits become curved, soft, rot rapidly with secondary microbes, and drop prematurely.
4) Economic Destruction: Causes massive direct yield destruction in bottle gourd orchards.
management:
1) Sanitation: Collect and bury infested or dropped fruits in deep pits (at least 60 cm) to break pupation.
2) Pheromone Traps: Install Cue-lure methyl eugenol pheromone traps (4-6 traps/acre) to monitor and mass-trap male flies.
3) Fruit Bagging: Bag developing young gourds with breathable paper or fine mesh bags right after fruit set.
4) Poison Bait Spray: Spray bait consisting of Jaggery (100g) + Malathion 50 EC (10ml) in 10 liters of water on border plants.
5) Deep Summer Ploughing: Expose soil pupae to direct sun heat and predatory birds.

name: Aphids (Aphis gossypii)
causingAgent: Insects: Aphis gossypii (Melon / Cotton Aphid). Small pear-shaped soft-bodied insects multiplying in dense colonies on tender shoots.
favourableClimate: Mild to warm temperatures (20°C - 28°C) with dry spells and lush succulent vegetative growth.
symptoms:
1) Sap-Sucking Damage: Dense colonies on leaf undersides suck vital sap, causing leaves to curl downwards, crinkle, and yellow.
2) Honeydew & Sooty Mold: Excrete sticky honeydew attracting black sooty mold fungus that blocks sunlight.
3) Stunted Growth: Infested vines show stunted internodes, poor flowering, and reduced fruit set.
4) Viral Vector: Actively vectors debilitating cucurbit mosaic viruses.
management:
1) Natural Predators: Conserve ladybird beetles, hoverfly maggots, and lacewings.
2) Yellow Sticky Traps: Install yellow sticky cards (15-20/acre) to catch winged aphids.
3) Botanical Sprays: Spray Neem oil (5ml/L) or 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE).
4) Chemical Control: Spray systemic insecticides like Imidacloprid 17.8 SL (0.3 ml/L) or Thiamethoxam 25 WG (0.3 g/L) or Acetamiprid.
5) Companion Planting: Intercrop with flowering basil or marigold to repel pests.

name: Fusarium Wilt
causingAgent: Pathogen: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lagenariae. Soil-borne vascular fungal pathogen persisting for years in soil.
favourableClimate: Warm soil temperatures (25°C - 30°C / 77°F - 86°F), high soil moisture, and poor drainage.
symptoms:
1) Unilateral Wilting: Initial sudden wilting of leaves on one branch or side of the vine during warm sunny hours.
2) Progressive Chlorosis: Leaves turn dull yellow starting from lower crown leaves upwards.
3) Stunted Vine Growth: Affected plants stop growing, wither, and fail to produce viable gourds.
4) Vascular Browning: Longitudinal split of stem shows dark brown to reddish discoloration in xylem vessels.
management:
1) Resistant Varieties: Plant certified Fusarium wilt resistant bottle gourd hybrids.
2) Crop Rotation: Rotate 3-4 years with non-cucurbit crops (cereals, pulses, or brassicas).
3) Bio-fungicides: Inoculate soil with Trichoderma viride or T. harzianum (2.5 kg/ha with FYM) at sowing.
4) Soil Drenching: Drench collar root zone with Carbendazim (1 g/L) or Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L).
5) Raised Bed Planting: Cultivate on raised ridges with good drainage to prevent water stagnation.

name: Leaf Miner (Liriomyza spp.)
causingAgent: Insects: Leaf miners are larvae of small dipteran flies (Liriomyza spp.). Larvae tunnel through leaf mesophyll tissues.
favourableClimate: Warm temperate to tropical climates (22°C - 32°C) with abundant young, tender vine leaves.
symptoms:
1) Visible Serpentine Trails: Distinctive winding, silvery-white tunnels (mines) across the upper leaf surface.
2) Leaf Necrosis: Heavy tunneling causes leaf tissue to dry out, turn papery brown, and perish.
3) Reduced Plant Vitality: Drastic reduction in photosynthetic area weakens vines, causing flower shedding and poor fruit filling.
4) Stippling Marks: Tiny white puncture marks where adult flies feed on sap.
management:
1) Pruning: Handpick and destroy heavily mined lower leaves during early infestation.
2) Yellow Sticky Traps: Install yellow sticky cards at canopy height to capture adult flies.
3) Biological Control: Encourage eulophid parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea).
4) Targeted Insecticides: Apply translaminar insecticides such as Abamectin 1.9 EC (0.5 ml/L) or Cyromazine 75 WP or Spinosad 45 SC.
5) Reflective Mulches: Use silver reflective plastic mulch to deter adult flies from settling.

name: Leaf Spot (Cercospora / Alternaria)
causingAgent: Pathogens: Cercospora spp., Alternaria spp., and Rhizoctonia spp. Air-borne and rain-splashed fungal spores.
favourableClimate: Warm, humid weather (24°C - 32°C) with frequent rainfall, overhead irrigation, or heavy morning dew.
symptoms:
1) Circular Spots: Small circular to irregular spots on leaves with pale gray/tan centers and dark reddish-brown borders.
2) Concentric Zonation: Alternaria lesions display faint concentric target-like rings.
3) Leaf Distortion & Shot Holes: Dead centers of lesions may drop out leaving shot holes; leaves turn yellow and cup.
4) Premature Defoliation: Causes extensive leaf drop, exposing developing gourds to sunscald.
management:
1) Cultural Practices: Practice crop rotation, provide trellis spacing, and avoid overhead sprinkler watering.
2) Crop Sanitation: Remove and burn diseased plant residues after harvest.
3) Fungicides: Spray Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5 g/L), Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L), or Chlorothalonil (2 g/L) at 10-12 day intervals.
4) Seed Treatment: Treat seeds with Thiram or Captan (2.5 g/kg seed) before sowing.

name: Root Knot Nematode (Meloidogyne incognita)
causingAgent: Pathogen: Meloidogyne incognita. Microscopic soil-dwelling endoparasitic roundworms attacking root systems.
favourableClimate: Warm soil temperatures (15°C - 30°C / 60°F - 85°F), sandy or loamy soils, and continuous cucurbit cropping.
symptoms:
1) Root Galls & Knots: Diagnostic swollen knots, galls, and bead-like swellings throughout the root system.
2) Stunted Growth: Plants appear severely stunted, pale, and unthrifty.
3) Midday Wilting: Vines wilt rapidly during hot dry afternoons despite moist soil.
4) Severely Reduced Yield: Small deformed fruits and shortened harvesting lifespan.
management:
1) Crop Rotation: Rotate with non-host crops like marigold (Tagetes erecta) or sunn hemp to break nematode cycles.
2) Soil Solarization: Cover moist summer soil with transparent polythene sheets for 4-6 weeks.
3) Bio-nematicides: Apply Paecilomyces lilacinus or Pochonia chlamydosporia and Trichoderma viride enriched in FYM.
4) Nematicide Drenching: In severe cases, apply Fluopyram 34.48% SC or Cartap Hydrochloride as per label instructions.
5) Organic Soil Amendments: Apply Neem cake (250-500 kg/ha) during land preparation.

name: Downy Mildew
causingAgent: Pathogen: Pseudoperonospora cubensis. Oomycete foliar pathogen spreading rapidly via wind-blown sporangia.
favourableClimate: Warm, humid weather (18°C - 30°C / 60°F - 85°F) with heavy dew, rain, and poor air circulation.
symptoms:
1) Angular Yellow Spots: Bright yellow-green angular spots strictly delimited by veins on upper leaf surface.
2) Purple-Gray Downy Felt: Distinctive purplish-gray velvety downy coating on leaf underside in cool humid mornings.
3) Leaf Scorching & Necrosis: Infected areas turn brown, curl inward, and dry up rapidly like frost damage.
4) Premature Defoliation: Total loss of foliage canopy leading to fruit sunscald and immature fruit drop.
management:
1) Preventive Sprays: Apply Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5 g/L) or Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) preventively during rainy spells.
2) Curative Systemics: Spray Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (2.5 g/L) or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb or Dimethomorph (1 g/L).
3) Proper Spacing & Trellis: Maintain adequate spacing and trellising for maximum canopy aeration.
4) Drip Irrigation: Avoid overhead sprinklers; water at plant base.

name: Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
causingAgent: Insects: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf Whitefly). Minute sap-sucking pests that serve as major vectors for cucurbit viruses.
favourableClimate: Warm, dry, sunny weather (26°C - 36°C) with low rainfall.
symptoms:
1) Foliar Chlorosis: Sucking of sap causes chlorotic speckling, leaf yellowing, and vigor loss.
2) Sooty Mold: Heavy excretion of sticky honeydew encourages thick black sooty mold on foliage.
3) Viral Transmission: Vectors destructive Geminiviruses and Cucumber Green Mottle Mosaic Virus.
4) Stunted Vines: Heavy infestations stunt vine growth and reduce fruit set.
management:
1) Yellow Sticky Traps: Set up 20-25 yellow sticky cards per acre above the canopy.
2) Insecticide Sprays: Spray Diafenthiuron 50 WP (1 g/L), Pyriproxyfen 10 EC (1 ml/L), or Flonicamid 50 WG (0.3 g/L).
3) Botanical Sprays: Spray 5% NSKE or Neem oil (1500 ppm) at 7-10 day intervals.
4) Netting: Raise seedlings in protected insect-proof mesh nurseries.

name: Bacterial Wilt
causingAgent: Phytopathogenic vascular bacteria (Ralstonia solanacearum / Erwinia tracheiphila) transmitted by cucumber beetles and soil water.
favourableClimate: High temperatures (28°C - 35°C), high soil moisture, and waterlogged soil conditions.
symptoms:
1) Rapid Green Wilting: Leaves and vines wilt suddenly while remaining green without initial yellowing.
2) Bacterial Streaming: Slicing the stem base in clear water reveals milky white bacterial streaming threads.
3) Permanent Vine Collapse: Plants fail to recover overnight and die within 3-5 days.
4) Vascular Clogging: Bacterial slime completely clogs water transport in xylem vessels.
management:
1) Strict Vector Control: Control cucumber beetles and flea beetles that transmit the bacteria.
2) Raised Ridge Planting: Ensure excellent field drainage and avoid water stagnation.
3) Soil Drenching: Drench collar region with Streptocycline (0.1 g/L) + Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L).
4) Sanitation: Immediately uproot and burn infected vines; do not leave in field.
5) Resistant Rootstocks: Use certified disease-free seeds and resistant rootstocks.

name: Anthracnose (Colletotrichum orbiculare)
causingAgent: Pathogen: Colletotrichum orbiculare (syn. C. lagenarium). Fungal pathogen surviving in crop debris and infected seeds.
favourableClimate: Warm, rainy weather (22°C - 30°C) with relative humidity above 90% and splashing rain.
symptoms:
1) Water-soaked Spots: Small water-soaked circular lesions on leaves turning dark brown to black, often with yellow halos.
2) Stem Cankers: Sunken, dark brown elongated lesions on stems and petioles causing vine girdling.
3) Sunken Fruit Craters: Circular sunken dark lesions on gourds that develop pinkish gelatinous spore masses in humid weather.
4) Fruit Rotting: Infected gourds rot rapidly both in the field and during transit.
management:
1) Seed Treatment: Treat seeds with Carbendazim 50 WP (2 g/kg) or Captan (3 g/kg) before sowing.
2) Foliar Sprays: Apply Azoxystrobin 23 SC (1 ml/L), Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5 g/L), or Propiconazole 25 EC (1 ml/L).
3) Crop Rotation: Follow 2-3 year crop rotation with non-cucurbit crops.
4) Careful Handling: Avoid wounding gourds during harvest and packing.

name: Green Mirid Bug (Creontiades dilutus)
causingAgent: Insects: Creontiades dilutus / Campylomma spp. Slender pale-green plant bugs with piercing-sucking mouthparts feeding on buds and fruitlets.
favourableClimate: Warm, mild weather (22°C - 32°C) during peak flowering and young fruit development.
symptoms:
1) Blossom Abortion & Flower Drop: Bugs pierce tender flower buds, styles, and ovaries, causing buds to blacken and drop prematurely.
2) Fruitlet Dimpling & Deformity: Feeding punctures on tiny bottle gourds produce pimple-like bumps, resinous beads, and bent gourds.
3) Necrotic Leaf Punctures: Small pinprick necrotic holes on young expanding leaves.
4) Reduced Fruit Set: Heavy bug population drastically cuts marketable fruit yield.
management:
1) Field Scouting: Regularly inspect flower clusters in the early morning.
2) Companion Planting: Plant border trap crops to divert bugs from main field.
3) Targeted Sprays: Spray Spinetoram 11.7 SC (0.8 ml/L) or Flonicamid 50 WG (0.3 g/L) or Chlorantraniliprole 18.5 SC during pre-flowering and fruit set.
4) Neem Sprays: Apply 5% NSKE to deter feeding and oviposition.

name: Downy Mildew (Peronospora destructor)
causingAgent: Peronospora destructor. Destructive obligate oomycete foliar pathogen.
favourableClimate: Cool, humid, and wet conditions. Temperatures between 15°C to 22°C (59°F to 72°F) with high humidity, night fog, and morning dew.
symptoms:
1) Initial Pale Spots: Yellow to pale green oval spots appear on leaves, usually starting from tips or edges.
2) Purplish-Gray Mold: Spots enlarge and develop a diagnostic fuzzy gray or purplish downy mold growth on leaf undersides.
3) Severe Foliar Blight: Leaves become distorted, curl, collapse, and dry up prematurely, causing extensive defoliation.
4) Bulb Impact: Severely restricts bulb sizing, resulting in undersized, soft bulbs prone to storage rot.
management:
1) Crop Rotation: Avoid planting onions or related alliums in the same area consecutively for 3 years.
2) Proper Spacing: Adequate spacing (15x10 cm) promotes airflow and reduces moisture accumulation.
3) Good Drainage: Ensure proper field drainage to prevent waterlogging.
4) Resistant Varieties: Plant onion cultivars with downy mildew tolerance.
5) Fungicides: Spray Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5 g/L) or Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Copper Oxychloride.
6) Sanitation: Remove and destroy infected plant debris and volunteer onions.

name: Powdery Mildew (Leveillula taurica)
causingAgent: Fungus Leveillula taurica. Endophytic powdery mildew fungus with internal mycelium.
favourableClimate: Warm and dry conditions. Temperatures ranging between 20°C to 30°C (68°F to 86°F) with fluctuating humidity.
symptoms:
1) Initial White Patches: Powdery white to grayish patches appear on leaves and seed stalks, starting from older foliage.
2) Surface Progression: Patches spread across leaf surfaces, stems, and occasionally bulbs with a powdery white coating.
3) Leaf Damage: Leaves become distorted, turn yellow, scorch, and eventually die off prematurely.
4) Bulb Impact: In severe cases, bulb size and storage quality are substantially reduced.
management:
1) Proper Air Circulation: Plant onions with adequate spacing to ensure good airflow between rows.
2) Field Hygiene: Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest.
3) Avoid Overhead Irrigation: Minimize moisture on foliage by using drip or furrow irrigation.
4) Sulfur-Based Sprays: Apply Wettable Sulphur (2.5 g/L) or Sulfex at initial symptoms.
5) Systemic Fungicides: Spray Hexaconazole 5 EC (1 ml/L), Difenoconazole 25 EC (0.5 ml/L), or Azoxystrobin (1 ml/L).
6) Resistant Varieties: Plant powdery mildew tolerant onion varieties.

name: Purple Blotch (Alternaria porri)
causingAgent: Alternaria porri. Air-borne and seed-borne fungal pathogen.
favourableClimate: Warm and humid conditions. Temperatures ranging between 25°C to 30°C (77°F to 86°F) with high humidity >80%.
symptoms:
1) Water-soaked Lesions: Small water-soaked lesions with a purplish hue appear on leaves, starting from tips or edges.
2) Concentric Purple Spots: Lesions enlarge into distinct purplish-brown blotches with concentric rings and sunken centers.
3) Foliar Girdling: Severe infections cause leaves and seed stalks to girdle, collapse, and break over.
4) Bulb Neck Infection: Fungus penetrates bulb necks causing yellow-reddish watery rot during storage.
management:
1) Crop Rotation: Avoid planting onions or related alliums in the same location repeatedly.
2) Good Air Circulation: Adequate spacing between plants to ensure proper airflow and dry leaves quickly.
3) Remove Debris: Promptly remove and destroy infected plant material.
4) Fungicides: Spray Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5 g/L) + Sticker (0.5 ml/L), Chlorothalonil (2 g/L), or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L).
5) Thrips Control: Control onion thrips to prevent feeding wounds that allow Alternaria entry.
6) Proper Watering: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation.

name: Botrytis Leaf Blight (Botrytis squamosa)
causingAgent: Botrytis squamosa. Specialized foliar necrotic fungus producing sclerotia.
favourableClimate: Cool, humid, and wet conditions. Temperatures between 15°C to 25°C (59°F to 77°F) with high humidity.
symptoms:
1) Initial Flecks: Small water-soaked lesions appear on leaves, progressing to grayish-white fluffy or fuzzy patches with halos.
2) Leaf Progression: Patches spread across the leaf surface; lesions develop brownish margins and cause necrosis.
3) Extensive Defoliation: Severe infections cause extensive leaf dieback, weakening the plant.
4) Bulb Sizing Impact: Premature loss of green foliage severely limits bulb development.
management:
1) Proper Airflow: Ensure adequate spacing between onion plants to reduce humidity around foliage.
2) Avoid Overhead Irrigation: Use drip or furrow irrigation to minimize moisture on leaves.
3) Remove Infected Debris: Promptly remove and destroy infected plant residues.
4) Fungicides: Spray Iprodione 50 WP, Chlorothalonil 75 WP (2 g/L), or Boscalid + Pyraclostrobin.
5) Sanitation: Keep fields free of weeds to lower microclimate humidity.
6) Early Detection: Regularly monitor plants and spray at first sign of leaf flecks.

name: Neck Rot (Botrytis allii / Fusarium)
causingAgent: Botrytis allii, Fusarium species (such as Fusarium oxysporum), and secondary bacterial pathogens like Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
favourableClimate: Warm and humid conditions during maturity and storage. Excessive moisture during curing or high storage humidity.
symptoms:
1) Soft Watery Neck: Soft, watery lesions develop on the neck or upper part of onion bulbs.
2) Moldy Sunken Decay: Lesions progress to become moldy, soft, sunken, and emit a foul sour odor.
3) Storage Collapse: Grayish velvety mold with black sclerotia develops between scales; bulbs rot rapidly in storage bins.
4) High Post-Harvest Loss: Spreads rapidly between touching bulbs in poorly ventilated storage.
management:
1) Proper Harvesting: Harvest onions when 50-70% tops have lodged naturally and cure thoroughly before storage.
2) Adequate Curing: Dry onions thoroughly in a well-ventilated, dry area until necks are tightly sealed.
3) Avoid Bruising: Handle bulbs carefully to prevent physical injuries.
4) Storage Hygiene: Store in cool, dry conditions (0°C-2°C or well-aerated racks with 65-70% RH).
5) Sorting: Regularly inspect and sort stored onions; discard any soft or infected bulbs immediately.

name: Fusarium Basal Rot (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae)
causingAgent: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae. Soil-borne fungus persisting in soil and attacking basal plate.
favourableClimate: Spreads rapidly in warm soils with temperatures ranging between 24°C to 29°C (75°F to 85°F) and poor drainage.
symptoms:
1) Tip Yellowing & Wilting: Yellowing and progressive dieback of foliage starting from leaf tips downwards.
2) Basal Plate Decay: Reddish-brown discoloration and rotting at the basal plate and root attachment zone.
3) White/Pink Mold: Whitish or pinkish fungal mycelium visible on the decaying basal plate.
4) Bulb Damage: Significant reduction in bulb size and rapid soft rot breakdown during storage.
management:
1) Crop Rotation: Rotate 4-5 years with non-allium crops (wheat, maize, brassicas).
2) Soil Sanitation: Destroy infected crop debris; avoid waterlogging with raised beds.
3) Seed / Set Treatment: Treat onion sets or seeds with Trichoderma viride (10 g/kg) or Carbendazim (2 g/kg).
4) Soil Drenching: Drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) or Carbendazim.
5) Resistant Cultivars: Plant onion varieties bred with basal rot tolerance.

name: Fusarium Wilt
causingAgent: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae. Soil-borne vascular fungus penetrating through roots.
favourableClimate: Warm soil temperatures (24°C to 29°C / 75°F to 85°F) and root-damaged fields.
symptoms:
1) Gradual Wilting: Leaves show gradual daytime wilting starting with older leaves even with adequate soil moisture.
2) Interveinal Chlorosis: Foliage turns yellow between veins and collapses.
3) Stunted Vigor: Infected plants exhibit stunted growth, thin neck development, and poor vigor.
4) Vascular Discoloration: Slicing stems reveals brown or reddish vascular discoloration.
management:
1) Crop Rotation: Avoid planting onions or related crops in the same area consecutively.
2) Soil Health & Bio-control: Enrich soil with FYM inoculated with Trichoderma and Pseudomonas fluorescens.
3) Sanitation: Remove and destroy infected plant material.
4) Seedling Treatment: Dip seedling roots in bio-fungicide solution before transplanting.
5) Soil Solarization: Solarize nursery beds under transparent polythene during summer.

name: Bacterial Bulb Rot (Pseudomonas / Burkholderia)
causingAgent: Bacterial pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burkholderia cepacia, and Pectobacterium carotovorum.
favourableClimate: Warm and moist conditions (28°C - 35°C), high humidity, rain near harvest, and excessive moisture around bulbs.
symptoms:
1) Water-soaked Slimy Scales: Infected bulbs develop soft, water-soaked, slimy lesions on inner scales while outer scales look normal.
2) Repulsive Odor: Rotting bulbs emit a strong, foul sour odor.
3) Slippery Core: Squeezing the bulb neck causes the soft rotten core to slide out.
4) Fast Storage Spread: Rapidly infects neighboring bulbs in humid storage crates.
management:
1) Avoid Overhead Sprinklers: Use drip or furrow irrigation to keep foliage and bulb necks dry.
2) Thorough Curing: Ensure complete drying and curing of necks before storage.
3) Sorting: Inspect stored onions regularly and promptly discard any soft or diseased bulbs.
4) Prevent Bruising: Handle bulbs gently to avoid skin cuts and bruises.
5) Proper Storage: Store in cool (0°C-2°C), dry, well-ventilated storage rooms with 65-70% humidity.
